newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU industry liberalisation slow in some sectors.
newsitem.headline: EU industry liberalisation slow in some sectors.

text.p: For the best part of a decade, the European Union has been trying to break the grip of state monopolies on key industries, hoping to build a more efficient economy that can compete with the United States and Japan.
But the private sector and some governments say the drive is slowing and want to see faster progress in opening up protected sectors to cross-border competition.
The EU has set a January 1, 1998, deadline for abolishing state telecoms monopolies in most of its 15 member states and will complete deregulation of its aviation market this year.
But there has been at best limited progress in liberalising other sectors, such as postal services and energy, reflecting fears in some countries that it could lead to more lost jobs.
"The current weather conditions for liberalisation are not good," EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told a recent conference.
"Of course one would like it to move a lot more quickly," said Keith Richardson, secretary-general of the European Round Table of Industrialists.

The EU's unemployment rate of 11 percent and the prospect of widespread strikes at a time when EU countries are struggling to rein in their budgets to qualify for the single currency have created a climate that is not conducive to significant reforms.
EU countries are preoccupied by Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), said Stanley Crossick, chairman of the European Policy Centre, a Brussels-based think tank.
"In terms of competitiveness we have a long way to go in Europe and any delay in achieving that competitiveness, any delay in liberalisation therefore is unsatisfactory," he said.
"Having said that, there is no doubt that monetary union is the number one priority," Crossick added.
SENSITIVE SECTORS LEFT TO LAST

The difficulties were demonstrated in December when EU telecommunications ministers decided to delay significant liberalisation of postal services -- which employ more than one million people across the EU -- until at least 2003.
France led a heavy lobbying campaign to postpone plans to allow private operators to carry direct mail and cross-border mail -- and won surprise support from Germany.

One reason why liberalisation may be becoming more difficult is that the EU first tackled the relatively easy sectors in the run-up or following the launch in 1993 of its single market -- which broke down internal barriers to trade -- while now it is left with the the more sensitive ones.

The sectors still closed to competition are characterised by "hard core vested interests, hard core state monopolies that have to be broken," Crossick said. "So the pace in doing this is going to be slower."
Anton van der Lande, secretary-general of the European Express Organisation (EEO), said the trend in liberalising the postal sector had been positive until 1992.
But now "this whole process has not only been delayed, as far as I can see it has stopped completely," he said.
A deal last year on liberalising electricity markets will benefit mainly large industrial consumers and not households.
"It is a good move in the right direction but it didn't go far enough," said Katrin Schweren, economic adviser at the European Consumers' Organisation.
The views on deregulation vary among member states with Britain and the Nordic countries pushing for liberalisation, while France and Belgium are more sceptical.
Those wary of liberalisation fear it would disturb the provision of essential services, such as electricity, to everybody at an affordable price regardless of where they live.

There are more and more discussions about "the concept of public services which might be approached in such a way that the liberalisation is slowed down," said Daniel Cloquet, director of industrial affairs at UNICE, the European employers' group.
But, he said, "in our view maintaining monopolies is not at all the right solution for public service issues."
LIBERALISATION SEEN BOOSTING COMPETITIVENESS
However, those advocating liberalisation also point to the gains that have been made in the telecommunications, aviation and electricity sectors.
"It would always be nice to go further and faster," said a British EU diplomat. But, he added, "any progress, even if it is on a very small scale, is better than no progress."

Jacques Pelkmans, senior research fellow at the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), noted that much had changed since the mid-80s, when state monopolies were the norm. "If you come from that position I think we have moved quite far."
The European Commission and industry argue that liberalisation helps to cut costs and spur innovation, crucial elements in boosting the continent's competitive strength.
"The one who is defending monopolies is in fact defending unemployment," said EU Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann.

A 1996 report by the EU executive said the 15-nation bloc continued to lag behind the United States in labour productivity, with the result that its per capita gross domestic product was almost one third lower.
EU industry also faces higher costs for inputs such as energy.

"Prices for key service inputs in Europe have remained higher than those of major competitors and with the progress of liberalisation elsewhere the gap between Europe and major competitors has been widening," the report said.
"If you want to find arguments for further liberalisation, they are there," said Pelkmans at CEPS.
The European Federation of Public Service Unions (EPSU), representing 160 trade unions organising 11 million public service workers in Europe, thinks differently.
Reacting angrily to last year's EU agreement on a limited liberalisation of electricity markets, it said 200,000 jobs had been lost in the sector since 1990, partly due to deregulation.
EPSU official Jan Willem Goudriaan accused the Commission of not taking into account the social consequences of its policies.

He rejected the view that deregulation would help solve Europe's unemployment problem. "I don't have to remind you that despite this policy over the last 10 years we still have 18 million unemployed in Europe," he said.
